paragraphs: The Sovereign has no force except the legislative power, so it acts only through the laws. The laws are nothing but the authentic acts of the general will, so the Sovereign can act only when the people is assembled. A people in assembly, I shall be told, is a mere fantasy. Today it is. Two thousand years ago it was not. Has human nature changed?

In moral matters, the bounds of what is possible are less narrow than we imagine; it is our weaknesses, our vices and our prejudices that confine them. Base souls do not believe in great men; vile slaves sneer at the very name of liberty.

Let us judge what can be done by looking at what has been done. I shall say nothing of the Republics of ancient Greece. But in my view the Roman Republic was a great State, and Rome a great city. The last census found four hundred thousand citizens in Rome able to bear arms, and the last count of the Empire’s population came to over four million citizens, not counting subjects, foreigners, women, children and slaves.

What difficulties might one not suppose to stand in the way of frequently gathering the vast population of that capital and its surroundings. Yet few weeks went by without the Roman people meeting in assembly, and even several times. They exercised not only the rights of Sovereignty but part of those of government as well. They dealt with certain matters and judged certain cases, and this whole people was found in the public meeting-place almost as often in the role of magistrates as in that of citizens.

If we went back to the earliest history of nations, we would find that most ancient governments, even monarchies such as the Macedonian and the Frankish, held similar councils. In any case, the one undeniable fact I have given answers every objection; to reason from what has actually happened to what is possible is sound logic.
